concepts.title: The Family: Basic Unit of Society

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Family: Basic Unit of Society' refers to.
questions.a: The family is the fundamental and most ancient unit of society, where children are born, nurtured and taught values; Indian families range from joint households to nuclear ones.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Family: Basic Unit of Society'.
questions.a: Society is built family by family: the first lessons of living together are learned at home.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Family: Basic Unit of Society' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Joint and Nuclear Families' refers to.
questions.a: A joint family keeps several generations under one roof, grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins, while a nuclear family is only a couple with their children; Indian languages even name relations that English must borrow words for.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Joint and Nuclear Families'.
questions.a: Family shape changes but the web of relations stays dense: bua, tau, chacha and nani name bonds that matter.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Joint and Nuclear Families' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Dharma and Values within the Family

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Dharma and Values within the Family' refers to.
questions.a: The family is a school of values where children learn ahimsa, dana, seva and tyaga; in the story, Shalini gives up her expected silk dress so the whole family can share clothes for Onam with her uncle's household.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Dharma and Values within the Family'.
questions.a: Following dharma in a family often means giving up a small wish so that others are not left out.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Dharma and Values within the Family' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Values and the Shalini story (source: fees109.txt, Values and the Shalini story)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Community: Beyond the Family' refers to.
questions.a: Beyond kin, people live in communities bound by place, work or faith, jatis and neighbourhoods, temples and schools; a community shares joys, helps in trouble and sets some rules of its own.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Community: Beyond the Family'.
questions.a: Community extends the family's care: neighbours and fellow members become a wider circle of support.
